docs.markdown: # Klarbefund user guide Klarbefund turns a paper lab report into values you can read, check against the paper, and follow over time. Everything runs on the phone: the scan, the reading, the coding, the store and the exports. Nothing needs an account, and nothing leaves the device unless you send it. This guide walks through the app as a person uses it, task by task. The developer side (building, testing, the shared dictionary, the store layout) is the [developer guide](/docs/klarbefund/klarbefund-developer-guide). The work is tracked in [issue #186](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/issues/186). Every screenshot in this guide shows invented data. The laboratory, the practice, the patient and every number come from the app's own fictional development dataset, so a screenshot can be published without a real report ever being involved. How they are made is at the [end of this guide](#how-these-screenshots-are-made). | App name | Klarbefund, in English and German | | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Runs on | iPhone, iOS 26 or later | | Get it | [Public TestFlight beta](https://testflight.apple.com/join/ssADSXX6), 200 places | | Languages | English and German, following the phone's language | | Source | [`clients/ios/`](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/tree/main/clients/ios) | | Privacy | [Privacy policy](https://ma3u.github.io/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/meinbefund/privacy.html) | | Not | a medical device: it explains what a measurement is and never judges a value ([below](#not-a-medical-device)) | ## Getting started 1. On the iPhone, open the [TestFlight link](https://testflight.apple.com/join/ssADSXX6). TestFlight installs itself first if it is missing, then offers Klarbefund. 2. Open Klarbefund. There is no sign-up and no account: the app is ready for the first scan. 3. The first time you scan, iOS asks for the camera. The app uses it only for the pages of a report and for the QR code that connects it to your record; the photographs stay on the phone. **The lock.** By default the app asks for Face ID, Touch ID or the passcode every time it comes to the front, so your results are not on show to whoever holds the unlocked phone. The switch is under **Analysis provider** in the **⋯** menu, section **Protection**. A phone without a passcode has nothing to ask for, and the lock then opens by itself. ## Your reports The home screen lists every report, newest first: the title, the laboratory, practice or device it came from, the date it was taken and how many values were read. **1 to review** marks a report with a value you have not yet checked against the paper. The coloured badge is the report's **provenance**, and it matters more than it looks. **Lab-issued, final** means the values came out of a PDF that carried the laboratory's own text, so nothing was guessed. **Scanned, preliminary** means the values were read from a photograph, of a paper sheet or of a device's screen, and a photograph can be misread. A value stays preliminary until you have checked it against the original. The **+** button starts a scan or an import. The **⋯** button holds everything else: trends, reference values, your profile, earlier measurements, consents, the connection to the EHDS, exports, privacy and the analysis provider. ## Getting a report in There are three ways, and the document decides what its values are worth. - **Scan report** opens the camera for a paper report. The app finds the page edges, reads the table on the device, and keeps the pages as a PDF next to the values. Multi-page reports are fine. - **Import a PDF or photo** takes a file your laboratory or portal gave you. If the PDF carries the laboratory's own text layer, the values are marked final; a PDF that is only a picture goes through the recogniser like a scan. - **Import from Photos** takes photographs already on the phone, up to twelve at a time. The app reads more than laboratory sheets. A **24-hour blood pressure measurement**, a **resting or exercise ECG**, a **Holter report**, a **spirometry**, a **lactate test**, a **CGM glucose profile**, a **DXA scan** and a **gut microbiome analysis** each have their own reader, so the values a practice prints on those sheets arrive with the right codes and units. A **body-composition scale** photographed in a gym is recognised as what it is: a dashboard, not a report. The app reads the metric, its current value and the date the scale shows, and where the scale plots a history it measures the points on the chart and marks those values as estimates. The scale's own verdicts ("Normal", "Low") are ignored; they are the manufacturer's bands, not a guideline's. Before anything is saved, the app shows what it read and asks you to confirm the laboratory date it found on the sheet. A report that looks like one you already have is pointed out; **Find duplicate reports** in the menu does the same for the whole list later. ## Checking a report, value by value The top of a report is what the app read from the sheet's header: the laboratory, the date the sample was taken, the date the report was issued, the report number, and a link to the original pages. Then every measurement, and under each one the four things that make it checkable: - **the LOINC code** it was matched to, so the value means the same thing in every system it is exported to. The unit picks the code, never the name: lipoprotein(a) in mg/dL and in nmol/L are different measurements with different codes. A quantity LOINC does not code says so plainly instead of showing a near-enough code, and an organism from a stool report shows its NCBI Taxonomy id instead, because LOINC names tests and not organisms; - **the reference range your laboratory printed**, exactly as printed, never normalised; - **the page and line** it was read from, so any number can be checked against the paper in front of you; - **the published band**, where a guideline or a named study states one, with the words and a symbol beside the colour: "in the optimal band", "outside the optimal band", "outside the guideline range". This is a comparison to a number somebody published. It is not a finding. **Checking against the paper.** Tap a value to correct its name, number or unit; the correction is kept beside what the recogniser read, so the paper trail stays. **Mark all values as checked** turns the report's values from preliminary into checked once you have compared them. A report with values still to check carries **to review** in the list. Below the recognised values come two lists the app never hides: the lines that looked like measurements but matched nothing in the dictionary, and the lines that could not be read at all. A row that vanished silently would be indistinguishable from a row that was never printed, so no row vanishes. **Report missing values** in the report's menu sends the developers the labels of such rows, never the values, so the dictionary can grow. The share button offers the exports described further down. The menu lets you read the report again with the current version of the reader, scan the paper again, edit its name and laboratory, export its diagnostics, or delete it. ## The original pages Every report keeps its pages, as one PDF, encrypted like the values. **Original scan** shows them back, so the source is always one tap away from the reading. ## Trends **Trends** draws one chart per measurement across every report, ordered by what is furthest from its range. The filters narrow it to what matters: only analytes measured more than once, or only those outside a band. Each chart says what it is showing. Every kind of evidence has its own shape: a circle came from a laboratory's own file, a diamond was read from a photograph and is preliminary, and a triangle was entered by you or taken from a device. A legend under every chart that mixes them names each shape in words, so nothing depends on colour or on tapping a point. The green band is the published optimal band where one exists; for everything else the band drawn is the range your own laboratory printed, in its own colour and named as such. Under the chart every point is listed with its date, where it came from and which report it belongs to, and tapping a point opens that report. A sentence under each chart says **what the measurement is**: a definition of the test, in English or German. It is never a reading of your own value. At the bottom, **Show trends from Apple Health** reads your resting heart rate, heart rate variability, steps and weight, after asking once for permission. They appear in their own section, **From your devices**, as grey dashed lines of weekly means on the same months as your reports, with a thin blue line on each report's day so the two can be read against each other. They are never drawn as a lab value: no range, no comparison, no colour that means anything, and they go into no export. The app reads them while the screen is open, writes nothing to Health and keeps no copy. ## Reference values **Reference values** is the table behind the bands. One card per measurement, a line per unit, two columns: **Guideline**, the threshold a guideline body states for adults, and **Optimal**, the lowest-risk band the same source names. Every card names its source and links to it; where a source partitions by risk tier or by age, the card says so and leaves the choice of tier to a clinician. A measurement with no citable source is simply absent. That is the difference from the longevity tables this screen was modelled on, which quote numbers nobody can check. The category menu narrows the list to one panel, and setting your sex in the profile adds the ranges that differ by sex. ## Profile and earlier measurements The **profile** holds sex, date of birth and height, used only to pick the published ranges that apply to you, and the body measurements: waist, weight and visceral fat. Each measurement keeps its own date and says where it came from. A value read from a scale's photograph is labelled as such; one you type is labelled as entered by you. **Earlier measurements** is for catching up: one date per line, with whatever you measured that day. Saving stores each date as its own report, marked as entered by you, and works out the BMI and waist-to-height ratio from the height in the profile. They join the trends and the exports through the same path as a laboratory's values. ## Asking what a value is You can ask the app to explain a set of values. By default the model on the iPhone answers, so the question never reaches a network at all. If you would rather use a service, you pick the values, see them listed with their codes, and confirm before anything is sent. Only those values and your question travel. Your name, date of birth and insurance number are never sent, because the app does not hold them; they may be printed on the scanned page, which stays on the phone. Whichever provider is in use is named on the screen before you send. **Analysis provider** in the menu chooses where an answer comes from: on this iPhone, the Klarbefund service in the EU, or your own Azure OpenAI resource or Anthropic key. With your own service the phone talks to it directly, and neither the key nor the values reach the provider of this app. The same screen holds the **Protection** switch for the Face ID lock. ## Consents **Consents**, in the menu, keeps your own record of three decisions that are easy to confuse and must never be one switch: - **Study participation**, your consent to a study, held by the study centre; - **Electronic patient record (ePA)**, an _objection_, because the ePA exists unless you object to your health insurer; - **Registry and research use**, your consent for a registry or research database to use your values. Each has its own state, date, holder and button, and changing one never changes another. Withdrawing keeps the earlier grant in the history, so you can still show when you gave it. The app tells nobody: to give or withdraw one, contact whoever holds it. Two places use the record. **Export for research** asks once before exporting when no registry consent is recorded, and **Share for my doctor** reminds you, when you recorded an objection to the ePA, that there is no ePA to upload to while it stands. ## Connect to EHDS **Connect to EHDS**, in the menu, connects the app to your record in the European Health Data Space demo hub, so it can read it and, if you decide so, add to it. There are three ways in, and no password is typed into a web page on the phone: - **Create an EHDS account** makes an account with its own, empty record on the demo hub and connects the phone to it. You get a username and password to sign in on the website too. Apple confirms to the hub that the request comes from the genuine app on a real device, which is why a simulator cannot do this. - **Sign in with an EHDS account** you already have. - **Connect by QR code**, from the patient screen on a computer: 1. On the computer, open the patient screen (the app shows the address, to copy, share or open) and sign in as a patient. Choose **Show QR code**. 2. In the app, **Scan QR code**. On the computer, **Approve on this computer** opens Keycloak's consent page; check that the code shown there is the one the app shows, and approve. 3. The app says which account it connected to and asks **Is this your account?** A code someone else showed you would connect the phone to their account, so if the name is not yours, choose **Not me, disconnect**. Once connected, **Show my EHDS record** lists what the hub holds for you: measurements with their printed ranges and dates, reports, vaccinations and the medication plan. On the demo hub every record is synthetic, and the screen says so. The record is read when you open it, kept nowhere, and never mixed into your scanned reports. Two switches decide what goes the other way, and both are off until you turn them on: - **Send my reports to my EHDS record**: while it is on, every report you scan or read again goes to your own record, as preliminary values marked as read from a scan. Values without a LOINC code stay on the phone. - **Send my device trends to my EHDS record**: the weekly means from Apple Health that the Trends screen shows, never a single day or a single reading; each sync replaces the last. Switching either off stops further sending; what was sent stays in the record until you delete the account. **Disconnect** is in the app and on the patient screen, where every connected phone is listed. On a phone holding the patient screen itself, **Open in Klarbefund** does the same as the QR code, and the iPhone's camera app opens Klarbefund from the code too. The code works once, for two minutes. ## Exports and your data rights Everything the app holds can leave it, in the form the recipient needs, and only when you say so. | Action | For | What you get | | -------------------------- | ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Share for my doctor | a practice, the ePA | a PDF summary with the original pages appended, plus a FHIR R4 bundle | | Export for research (OMOP) | an analytics team | OMOP CDM v5.4 `measurement.csv`, `person.csv`, `observation_period.csv` | | Export all my data | you, under GDPR | every report, page, value, profile field and consent, in one archive | | Delete all my data | you | the store is wiped for good, and the app says so before it does it | | Export diagnostics | the developers | the recognised text and both recogniser passes, to fix a misread line | The FHIR bundle carries every value with its LOINC code, its UCUM unit, the range the laboratory printed (as numbers where they can be read, and always as the printed text in `referenceRange.text`), and the page and line it was read from. A value read from a photograph is marked preliminary in the bundle too. The doctor export fits the ePA's 25 MB limit with the pages attached. Everything goes through the system share sheet: to the ePA app, Files, AirDrop, or mail. There is deliberately no upload of its own, because there is no API into the ePA for an app like this, and the citizen is the integration point. ## Privacy and safety The photographs never leave the device. Values, pages and diagnostics are encrypted individually with a key that is unavailable while the phone is locked and is never restored onto another device. The store is excluded from iCloud Backup. When the app is not in front, its content is covered, so the app switcher shows nothing, and coming back asks for Face ID or the passcode. This was checked, not assumed: with the phone on a cable, copying a stored record, an export left in the temporary folder, or the system's own snapshot of the app all fail with a permission error, which is what complete file protection looks like from outside. The full assessment, objective by objective, is the [self-assessment](/docs/security/klarbefund-self-assessment); what was tested and how is in [evidence](/docs/security/klarbefund-evidence). ## Not a medical device Klarbefund explains what a measurement is. It does not diagnose, does not assess your risk and does not recommend treatment. No screen says normal or abnormal, scores anything, or advises. A value read from a photograph can be misread and is marked preliminary until you check it against the paper. Reference ranges are shown exactly as your laboratory printed them, and the published bands beside them are quotations with a source, not a verdict. Always consult a doctor before making any decision about your health. ## When something is read wrong A recogniser reads a photograph, and photographs get misread. Three things help, in this order: 1. **Compare with the paper.** The page and line under every value is there for this. Tap the value to correct it; the correction is kept beside the reading. 2. **Read again with this version**, in the report's menu, after an app update: the pages are kept, so a better reader can read them again. A re-read that finds fewer values than are stored is discarded, never saved over the better reading. 3. **Report missing values**, in the report's menu, sends the labels of the rows the app could not code, never your numbers, so the dictionary can learn the laboratory's spelling. **Export diagnostics** hands you an archive with the recognised text to attach to an [issue](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/issues/186); it leaves the phone only through the share sheet, when you send it. ## How these screenshots are made The images in this guide are shot from a simulator by [`clients/ios/Scripts/capture-screenshots.sh`](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/clients/ios/Scripts/capture-screenshots.sh), launching the app straight into each screen with the fictional development dataset: ```bash cd clients/ios SEED=-MBDevData OUT=/tmp/shots \ SCREENS="list detail scan trends reference history profile consent settings privacy consents connect" \ Scripts/capture-screenshots.sh for f in /tmp/shots/*.png; do sips --resampleWidth 660 "$f" --out "../../docs/klarbefund/img/$(basename "$f")"; done ``` The dataset is built in code, in memory, and is compiled out of a release build. Every laboratory and practice in it is invented and every value made up, which is the only reason a screenshot may be committed at all: the rule in the [developer guide](/docs/klarbefund/klarbefund-developer-guide#two-rules-that-are-not-negotiable) is that no real health data enters the repository, not even as a picture, not even temporarily.

docs.markdown: # Klarbefund developer guide How to build, run, test and change the iPhone app in [`clients/ios/`](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/tree/main/clients/ios). The [user guide](/docs/klarbefund/klarbefund-user-guide) shows what a person sees; this guide shows what makes it so. The short command card is [`clients/ios/README.md`](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/clients/ios/README.md); the work is tracked in [issue #186](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/issues/186). Every screenshot and every number in this guide comes from the app's own fictional development dataset. No real report is involved anywhere in the repository, and [the two rules at the end](#two-rules-that-are-not-negotiable) say why that is not negotiable. ## What you need | Tool | Version | Why | | ------------------ | ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | macOS with Xcode | Xcode 27, iOS 26 SDK | The app targets iOS 26; the Swift package declares macOS 26 for the tools | | Swift | 6.0, strict concurrency | `Package.swift` and `project.yml` both pin it | | XcodeGen | `brew install xcodegen` | The `.xcodeproj` is generated from `project.yml` and never committed | | Node | as for `ui/` | Only to regenerate the dictionary from `services/epa-ingest` | | PlantUML, Graphviz | `brew install plantuml` | Only to re-render the diagrams in this guide | | An iPhone | iOS 26 or later | Only for the camera, Face ID, App Attest and TestFlight; everything else runs in the simulator | ## How it is put together ![Klarbefund as an ArchiMate layered view: the business layer with the person, the doctor and the research team and the six things a person does; the application layer with the four services, the app, the Shared package, the tools, the hub and the generator; the technology layer with the iPhone's frameworks, the Mac and Azure Container Apps](__BASE_PATH__/published-docs/klarbefund-architecture.svg) Source: [`diagrams/klarbefund-architecture.puml`](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/klarbefund/diagrams/klarbefund-architecture.puml), rendered with `scripts/render-plantuml.sh docs/klarbefund/diagrams/*.puml`. The view follows ArchiMate 3.2: the business layer (yellow) holds who does what, the application layer (blue) the services the software provides and the components that realise them, the technology layer (green) what it all runs on. An arrow from a lower band to an upper one means "serves"; a dotted arrow with a hollow head means "realises". Three things to read off it: - **`Sources/Shared`** is a Swift package that compiles for iOS and macOS. It holds the parser, the recogniser's post-processing, the generated analyte dictionary and reference ranges, the record model with its provenance, and the export formats (FHIR R4, OMOP CDM, the diagnostics bundle). Nothing in it touches the network, the Keychain or the store, which is why every number the app computes can be reproduced on a Mac with `swift test`. - **`Sources/MeinBefund`** is the app: SwiftUI views, VisionKit scanning, the sealed store, the exports' share sheet, the EHDS connection, the app lock, the analysis providers, and the debug-only demo data and self-test. - **`Tools/`** are four command-line programs over the Shared package: `LabFile` imports a PDF or image exactly as the app would, `ScanReplay` re-runs a diagnostics export through the current parser, `AnalyteParity` proves the generated dictionary equals its TypeScript source, and `IconGen` draws the app icon. ``` clients/ios/ project.yml XcodeGen spec: the Shared framework and the MeinBefund app Package.swift SwiftPM: Shared, the four tools, SharedTests Sources/Shared/ parser, provenance model, formats; *.generated.swift are generated Sources/MeinBefund/ the app; en.lproj and de.lproj hold the strings Tools/{LabFile,ScanReplay,AnalyteParity,IconGen}/ Tests/SharedTests/ Swift Testing: what the app computes Tests/UITests/ XCUITest: what it shows, and what a tap does Scripts/ build, install, upload, screenshots, localisation, CodeQL appstore/ App Store Connect texts and the screenshot upload ``` ## Build and run ```bash cd clients/ios brew install xcodegen # once swift test # the Shared package, on the Mac swift run AnalyteParity # the generated table agrees with its source xcodegen generate && open MeinBefund.xcodeproj # then run the MeinBefund scheme in Xcode ``` From the command line into a simulator, note the **ad-hoc signature**: without it every Keychain call fails with `-34018` and the store cannot create its key. ```bash xcodebuild -project MeinBefund.xcodeproj -scheme MeinBefund \ -sdk iphonesimulator -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro' \ CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY="-" CODE_SIGNING_REQUIRED=YES build ``` Onto a connected iPhone: `Scripts/install-device.sh`. The generated project carries no signing team, so a plain `xcodebuild` for a device fails; the script supplies one from `TEAM_ID` or from the keychain, and installs what it built. TestFlight: `Scripts/archive-and-upload.sh`; its header names the four things that must exist in the Apple Developer account first. The version is pinned in `project.yml`: `MARKETING_VERSION` matches the App Store Connect record and `CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION` rises with every upload, because App Store Connect refuses a build number it has already seen, after the upload. ## Demo data and launch arguments Every launch argument below exists only in a Debug build. The checks are `#if DEBUG`, not a flag alone: a flag can be discovered, code that is not compiled cannot. | Argument | What it does | | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `-MBDemoSeed` | Two fictional reports, in memory only. Enough for a screenshot; what every UI test launches with. | | `-MBDevData` | Seven fictional reports across three years and four sources, built in code: a trend has shape, the unmatched list has rows, every report has pages. | | `-MBShot ` | Opens a screen directly once the reports are loaded: `list detail scan trends reference history profile consent settings privacy consents connect`. | | `-MBSelfTest` | Drives one synthetic report through the whole pipeline in the app target and logs 27 checks (see [The self-test](#the-self-test)). | | `-MBExportDiagnostics` | Builds the diagnostics archive into the app's temporary directory for `Scripts/pull-diagnostics.sh`. | The dev dataset is **built, not stored**. A row states the label, the value, the unit and the range the laboratory printed, and `Analytes.lookup` codes it exactly as it codes a scan. No code in the dataset can be wrong, a row the dictionary cannot code lands in the unmatched list of its own accord, and the dataset follows the dictionary when the dictionary changes. The pages are drawn by `SyntheticSheet`, the same renderer the tests read. A demo launch never locks: the app lock reads the seed flag and stays open, so the UI tests and the screenshot script run where nobody can answer a passcode prompt. On a release build neither the flag nor the exception exists. Screenshots for the documentation and the App Store come from one script, which launches each screen by argument rather than by scripted taps, so a re-shoot after a layout change needs no new coordinates: ```bash SEED=-MBDevData OUT=/tmp/shots SCREENS="list detail trends" Scripts/capture-screenshots.sh Scripts/capture-screenshots.sh # the App Store set, size-checked, into appstore/screenshots/en ``` ## From the camera to the store ![The scan pipeline as a sequence: the app's scanner hands the pages to LabImport, which decides the provenance, recognises or reads the text, reconciles the passes, infers the column roles, parses every row against the generated dictionary, reads the header, and hands the result to the review screen and then to the sealed store](__BASE_PATH__/published-docs/klarbefund-scan-pipeline.svg) Source: [`diagrams/klarbefund-scan-pipeline.puml`](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/klarbefund/diagrams/klarbefund-scan-pipeline.puml). The order is fixed and each step has one owner ([ADR-033](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-033-lab-report-extraction-pipeline.md)): 1. **Provenance first.** `LabImport` decides on the file, never its extension: a PDF carrying the laboratory's own text layer is `lab-issued-digital` and its Observations are `final`; anything that has to go through the recogniser is `ocr-transcribed` and `preliminary`. It is strict on purpose, because marking a transcription `final` is the failure that matters. 2. **Recognition.** `VisionDocumentReader` runs two Vision passes, German and English, with language correction **off**: "correcting" `Lp(a)` or a decimal comma is actively harmful. `DocumentReconciler` merges the passes and `TableRoles` infers which column holds the label, the value, the unit and the range, per table. 3. **Parsing.** `LabLineParser` reads every row. When the ordinary parse finds nothing, the sheet readers take their turn: ambulatory blood pressure, resting and exercise ECG, Holter, cardiopulmonary exercise test, lactate, CGM glucose profile, DXA, and a body-composition scale's screen, which is a dashboard and not a report and is read for its headline value only. 4. **Coding.** `Analytes.lookup(label, unit)` picks the LOINC code. The unit decides, never the name alone. A quantity LOINC does not code (visceral fat as a mass, a water ratio) is carried with its unit, no code and a required reason; an organism from a stool report carries its NCBI Taxonomy id, because LOINC names tests and not organisms. 5. **The header.** `ReportMetadata` and `PrintedFields` read the laboratory, the lab date, the issue date and the report number from the sheet; the lab date is preferred over the receipt and issue dates and the person confirms it before saving. 6. **Conservation.** Every row that looks like a measurement ends up coded, unmatched or unread. A row in none of the three is indistinguishable from a row that was never printed, and that is exactly how an HbA1c row went missing once (`docs/gotchas.md`, 2026-09-19). The self-test asserts it. 7. **Review and save.** `ReviewViews` shows what was read; `ReportStore` seals it. `swift run LabFile ~/Downloads/befund.pdf` runs steps 1 to 6 on a Mac and prints the provenance, the header, and every row as coded, unmatched or unread; `--values` adds the numbers, `--rows` adds the recogniser's layout. It refuses a path inside this repository. ## The store and the lock Three sealed files per report under `Application Support/Reports`, each AES-GCM under the same Keychain key, complete file protection, excluded from backup: ``` .sealed the record (LabReport) .scan.sealed the pages as one PDF .diag.sealed the scan's diagnostics (ScanDiagnostics) profile.sealed sex, date of birth, height (Profile) consents.sealed the three consent decisions (ConsentLedger) ``` The key is `ThisDeviceOnly` and unavailable while the phone is locked, so a container copy yields ciphertext and the system's own snapshot of the app fails with `EPERM`; `SecurityPostureTests` pins the build settings and the [self-assessment](/docs/security/klarbefund-self-assessment) records the measurement. Records written before a field existed still decode: every later field is optional or defaulted. The app lock ([ADR-060](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-060-the-app-locks-with-face-id-and-answers-pinning-and-jailbreak-detection.md)) is two types. `AppLockPolicy` in Shared decides _whether_ a challenge is due and is pure, so `AppLockPolicyTests` runs on a Mac; `AppLock` in the app asks LocalAuthentication _how_, Face ID, Touch ID or the passcode, and `PrivacyCover` draws the cover the app switcher sees. The same ADR says why certificate pinning and jailbreak detection were declined. ## The dictionary is generated, never copied `Sources/Shared/Analytes.generated.swift`, `ReferenceRanges.generated.swift` and `PromptText.generated.swift` are produced from [`services/epa-ingest`](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/tree/main/services/epa-ingest): ```bash cd services/epa-ingest && npm run generate:swift cd clients/ios && swift run AnalyteParity # 1589 codings, 71 units today ``` Do not hand-edit them. Add an analyte to `analytes.ts` or a range to `reference-ranges.ts`, regenerate, commit both. CI fails when a generated file is out of date with its source, because a stale copy is exactly the silent divergence the monorepo was chosen to prevent: an iPhone coding Lp(a) one way and the ingest service another, noticed when a value reaches a doctor. The reference-range generator refuses a range whose analyte the dictionary does not know or whose unit that analyte is not defined in. Only analytes with a citable published source get a band ([ADR-039](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-039-published-reference-ranges.md)); for every other analyte the Trends screen draws the range the person's own laboratory printed. ## Tests, and what each is for ```bash swift test # Swift Testing: what the app computes Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh # XCUITest: what it shows, and what a tap does swift test --filter ExtractionAccuracyTests # the accuracy benchmark, JSON to docs/klarbefund/accuracy-benchmark.json swift test --filter SecurityPostureTests # the build settings the self-assessment relies on ``` **The unit suite** (`Tests/SharedTests/`) is the larger one and catches what can be reasoned about: a unit that picks the wrong code, a date read from the wrong line, an export column in the wrong place. `FhirBundleParityTests` pins the bundle to the golden bundle `services/epa-ingest` writes, so both writers emit the same FHIR for the same sheet. **The UI suite** (`Tests/UITests/`) exists because the unit suite caught none of the last several defects: a card clipped at the chart's edge, a selection that forgot itself on the next render, `LOINC Optional("2093-3")` on the one screen a person compares with their own paper. Every test launches with `-MBDemoSeed` and reaches its screen with `-MBShot`, so it breaks when what it checks changes and not when a button moves. Three things learned the hard way are in `docs/gotchas.md`: an `accessibilityIdentifier` on a container renames everything inside it; a `Button` whose label is `Color.clear` is not in the accessibility tree; Swift Charts' selection answers a finger and not a synthesised tap, so real buttons sit over the marks. ### The self-test Everything after the camera runs in the app target and therefore not in `swift test`: the sealed store, the PDF of the pages, the export. `-MBSelfTest` drives one synthetic report through the whole chain and logs each of its 27 checks: recognition and coding, a citation per value, the lab date read from the header, the pages as a PDF, the three sealed files decrypting, the replay of the diagnostics record reproducing the extraction exactly, the archive building, and the doctor export fitting the ePA's 25 MB with the pages appended. ```bash xcrun simctl launch red.mabu.meinbefund -MBSelfTest xcrun simctl spawn log show --last 2m --predicate 'subsystem == "red.mabu.meinbefund"' --style compact ``` ### The accuracy benchmark `ExtractionAccuracyTests` reads synthetic sheets of known content and writes field-level accuracy to `docs/klarbefund/accuracy-benchmark.json`; the [evidence](/docs/security/klarbefund-evidence) page quotes it and [run-on-mac](/docs/security/klarbefund-run-on-mac) reproduces every number. A real report is measured the same way, on the person's own Mac and never in the repository, with `ScanReplay --truth` against a hand-written `truth.json` beside the export: it prints which fields of which rows were wrong, never the values. ## Debugging a misread sheet The store yields ciphertext, so evidence leaves the phone through the app's own **Export diagnostics**, which asks for confirmation in words and hands a zip to the share sheet ([ADR-038](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-038-scan-retained-diagnostics-export.md)): ``` klarbefund-diagnostics-/ about.json build, device, dictionary size, counts log.txt this session's log lines: counts and codes only -<id8>/ report.json the stored record: values, metadata, page text diagnostics.json both Vision passes, the reconciled rows, the layout scan.pdf the pages as scanned ``` With the phone on USB and a Debug build installed, `Scripts/pull-diagnostics.sh` does the export and the unzip in one go, under `~/Downloads`. Unzip **outside this repository**, then: ```bash swift run ScanReplay ~/Downloads/klarbefund-diagnostics-<date> # every report, with the current parser swift run ScanReplay ~/Downloads/klarbefund-diagnostics-<date> --ocr # re-run Vision on scan.pdf swift run ScanReplay ~/Downloads/klarbefund-diagnostics-<date> --truth # accuracy against truth.json ``` The replay prints what the phone coded, what codes now, what is newly coded or lost, and every row with its reason. Add an analyte to `analytes.ts`, regenerate, replay, and watch the real sheet's rows move from unmatched to coded without scanning it again. Both tools refuse a path inside `clients/ios/`. ## The connection to the EHDS hub The patient screen of the hub starts an OAuth 2.0 device grant for the public Keycloak client `klarbefund-app` and shows it as a QR code carrying a `klarbefund://connect` link; the app polls Keycloak for the token and registers with the hub ([ADR-049](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-049-klarbefund-connects-by-device-grant.md)). - `Shared/EHDSConnect.swift`: the link, refused unless its hub and issuer are on `TrustedHub.production` (plus `.development` in a debug build), and the poller with its four answers. `EHDSConnectTests` covers each. - `EHDSConnection.swift`: tokens and a device id in the Keychain as `ThisDeviceOnly`, refresh, register, read the record, disconnect (which revokes the refresh token at Keycloak), and the two sync switches. - `ConnectView.swift`: the sheet, VisionKit's data scanner for QR codes only, a paste field, and "Is this your account?". - **Create an EHDS account** ([ADR-054](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-054-klarbefund-creates-a-sandbox-account-with-app-attest.md)) calls the two routes on the hub that answer without a session; the account is created only for a request whose Apple App Attest attestation verifies, which is why the simulator shows the button disabled with its reason. - **Send my reports** and **Send my device trends** ([ADR-057](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-057-klarbefund-sends-weekly-device-means.md)) post to the person's own record; the record itself holds reports, vaccinations and the medication plan ([ADR-059](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-059-the-record-holds-reports-vaccinations-and-the-medication-plan.md)). - `ConnectUITests` and `AccountUITests` run against `DemoEHDSTransport` under `-MBDemoSeed`; `LiveConnectUITests` and `LiveAccountUITests` run against a real hub when given a fresh link (`docs/knowledge/runbooks/klarbefund-connect.md`). ## Exports | Action | Writer | Contents | | -------------------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Share for my doctor | `ReportExport`, `FhirBundle` | PDF summary with the original pages appended, plus a FHIR R4 bundle | | Export for research (OMOP) | `OmopExport` | OMOP CDM v5.4 `measurement.csv`, `person.csv`, `observation_period.csv` | | Export all my data | `DataExport` | every report, page, value, profile field and consent, as JSON and PDFs | | Export diagnostics | `DiagnosticsBundle` | the record, both Vision passes, the pages, the session log | The OMOP tables carry `measurement_concept_id = 0` throughout, deliberately: mapping LOINC to an OMOP concept needs the Athena vocabulary, which is not on a phone, and inventing an id would put a wrong identifier on a real measurement. The printed range is kept verbatim in `RawLabValue.referenceText` and travels as `referenceRange.text`; a range with no number in it survives only there, and FHIR's rng-2 allows that. ## Languages English is the base, German the translation, following the phone's language. `Scripts/check-localization.sh` fails when a user-visible string has no German or when a German sentence was left in the English base; it uses `xcodebuild -exportLocalizations`, the same extractor Xcode's editor uses, so it sees SwiftUI `Text` literals and `INFOPLIST_KEY_*` values that no grep of the sources would find. The camera permission prompt once shipped in German to every English phone, which is why the script exists. ## Static analysis and CI ```bash Scripts/codeql-swift.sh # CodeQL on the app and Shared, about 15 minutes ``` CodeQL needs a real build to see Swift, so on GitHub it runs only when `clients/ios/` changes (`.github/workflows/codeql-swift.yml`), on a macOS runner. The `codeql-swift` pre-push hook runs the same suite when a push changes the Swift sources; it exits 1 on any finding not listed, with its reason, in `Scripts/codeql-accepted.txt`. Swift needs a macOS runner, which has lower concurrency than Linux, so the iOS job is path-filtered to `clients/ios/**` and never gates the web or service suites; conversely, the `ui/**` and `services/**` workflows exclude `clients/ios/**`. The security posture of the app, its threat model and what an independent test would add are in the [threat model](/docs/security/threat-model-klarbefund), the [security test report](/docs/security/security-test-report) and the [self-assessment](/docs/security/klarbefund-self-assessment). ## Two rules that are not negotiable 1. **No health data in `clients/ios/`, ever.** No lab reports, no scans, no exported HealthKit archives, no screenshots containing real values, not even temporarily, not even gitignored. Test fixtures are synthetic, the way `services/epa-ingest/__tests__/fixtures/` already is. The tools refuse a path inside the repository for the same reason. 2. **No real organisation in demo content.** `CLAUDE.md` forbids it outside the `NEXT_PUBLIC_DEMO_TK` flag. The study this app is built for is real; the demo centre, the laboratory and the practice in the dev dataset are fictional. ## Where the decisions are | ADR | Decides | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | | [ADR-033](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-033-lab-report-extraction-pipeline.md) | The extraction pipeline and its order | | [ADR-038](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-038-scan-retained-diagnostics-export.md) | Diagnostics kept with the scan, exported on request | | [ADR-039](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-039-published-reference-ranges.md) | Only citable published ranges, beside the laboratory's own | | [ADR-049](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-049-klarbefund-connects-by-device-grant.md) | Connecting by OAuth device grant and QR code | | [ADR-050](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-050-klarbefund-beta-by-public-testflight-link.md) | The beta by public TestFlight link | | [ADR-054](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-054-klarbefund-creates-a-sandbox-account-with-app-attest.md) | Creating an account, gated by App Attest | | docs.markdown:
# Load, stress and spike tests: results and dashboards

What the live hub at https://ehds.mabu.red does under load, measured with the
k6 suite in [`load-tests/`](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/tree/main/load-tests) and recorded on the platform's
Grafana. This page is the index: every run, what it found, what changed
because of it, and the runs still to do. The detailed reports are linked, and
every live run has its dashboard link.

The dashboards need a sign-in on <https://grafana.ehds.mabu.red> and show
data only while the stack is up (it stops off hours, ADR-053). Each link
opens the **Load and stress test** dashboard on the run's `testid` and time
range; the raw k6 summaries are on the laptop that ran them
(`load-tests/results/<testid>*`) and in the issues.

| Scenario    | What it does                                                | Last run live     | Result                                                                  |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `smoke`     | 1 user, 30 s, every endpoint once                           | 2026-10-05        | passes                                                                  |
| `load`      | 50 users, 15 min, the persona mix                           | 2026-10-06, 21:15 | **passes every SLO**: p95 155 ms API, 43 ms pages, 217 ms NLQ, 0 failed |
| `audited`   | 1 to 20 parallel NLQ queries through the audit chain        | 2026-10-05        | passes after #534 and #536 (per-user rate limit)                        |
| `contracts` | up to 10 users negotiating and transferring through the EDC | 2026-10-06, 13:52 | passes: 578 requests, 0 failed, p95 287 ms                              |
| `stress`    | 50, 100, 200, 400 users, abort on failed requests           | 2026-10-06, 21:40 | **400 users, 0 failed**; latency SLOs break from 200 users, ceiling: UI |
| `spike`     | a sudden jump to many users and back                        | not yet           | next, after `size-ui.sh` (ADR-061)                                      |
| `soak`      | a steady load for two hours                                 | not yet           | after `spike`; measures the Postgres burst credits                      |
| `signin`    | 5 to 50 sign-ins a minute against Keycloak                  | not yet live      | compose: 12 of 127 sign-ins over 3 s                                    |
| `proxy`     | the proxy alone, 5 to 25 users                              | not yet live      | needs a job inside the environment; compose passes                      |

## The live runs, newest first

### 2026-10-06 evening: load and stress after the fixes of the day

Stack: Neo4j at 2 vCPU and 4 GiB (ADR-056), the graph views capped at the
newest 30 access events (#580), the onboarding agent's retry loop fixed (#581),
the task store on the Flexible Server (#589).

| Run                                                                                                                                                                       | Users             | Requests        | Failed     | p95 all / API / pages / NLQ       | Verdict                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------- | --------------- | ---------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [`20261006-2115-load-aca`](https://grafana.ehds.mabu.red/d/mvhd-load-test/load-and-stress-test?var-testid=20261006-2115-load-aca&from=1791321300000&to=1791322320000)     | 50 for 15 min     | 19,509 (21.5/s) | **0.00 %** | 146 ms / 155 ms / 43 ms / 217 ms  | every SLO held, checks 99.97 %                               |
| [`20261006-2140-stress-aca`](https://grafana.ehds.mabu.red/d/mvhd-load-test/load-and-stress-test?var-testid=20261006-2140-stress-aca&from=1791322800000&to=1791324300000) | 50 to 400, 20 min | 81,518 (63.6/s) | **0.00 %** | 3.35 s / 3.53 s / 3.23 s / 4.93 s | latency SLOs crossed from 200 users on; every answer correct |

The ceiling was the UI: three replicas of half a core at 99 % CPU from the
400-user stage on, Neo4j at 0.82 of its 2 cores and 2.66 GB of 4 GiB, the
proxy at 0.06 cores. The errors in the logs were the UI calling the EDC
management API at the wrong address (about 8,900 404 lines in the stress run),
which #648 pins on every deploy; the EDC pages did no real work in these runs,
so the next `load` after it moves the numbers.

What changed because of it: [ADR-061](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/ADRs/ADR-061-the-ui-scales-out-on-whole-cores.md),
a whole core per UI replica, up to six replicas on an HTTP concurrency rule of
15, applied by `scripts/azure/size-ui.sh`; a deploy now waits while a run is on
(`LOAD_TEST_RUNNING`), because a merge on 2026-10-06 redeployed the UI and the
proxy in the middle of a run.

### 2026-10-06 afternoon: the first stress run to 400 users

| Run                                                                                                                                                                       | Users         | Requests      | Failed           | p95 API / pages / NLQ        | Verdict                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- | ------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`20261006-1728-stress-aca`](https://grafana.ehds.mabu.red/d/mvhd-load-test/load-and-stress-test?var-testid=20261006-1728-stress-aca&from=1791307740000&to=1791309060000) | 50 to 400     | 84,624 (66/s) | **0.00 %**       | 3.19 s / 2.8 s / 4.35 s      | all stages reached; Neo4j did not restart after ADR-056             |
| [`20261006-1455-load-aca`](https://grafana.ehds.mabu.red/d/mvhd-load-test/load-and-stress-test?var-testid=20261006-1455-load-aca&from=1791298500000&to=1791299520000)     | 50 for 15 min | 10,000+       | 0.03 %           | pages and API under the SLOs | with #580 and #579 deployed; both audit chains intact after the run |
| [`20261006-1152-load-aca`](https://grafana.ehds.mabu.red/d/mvhd-load-test/load-and-stress-test?var-testid=20261006-1152-load-aca&from=1791287580000&to=1791288600000)     | 50 for 15 min |               | 0                | 151 ms overall               | with #576; ran beside the onboarding agent's retry loop (#577)      |
| [`20261006-stress-aca`](https://grafana.ehds.mabu.red/d/mvhd-load-test/load-and-stress-test?var-testid=20261006-stress-aca&from=1791274440000&to=1791275580000)           | 50 to 400     |               | 2.1 % at the end | `/api/graph` 64 s at the end | aborted at about 300 users: Neo4j killed for memory (exit 137)      |
| [`20261006-load-aca`](https://grafana.ehds.mabu.red/d/mvhd-load-test/load-and-stress-test?var-testid=20261006-load-aca&from=1791273300000&to=1791274320000)               | 50 for 15 min |               | 0                |                              | the morning baseline inside the environment                         |

The morning stress run found Neo4j's ceiling by memory; the afternoon run,
after `size-neo4j.sh` (2 vCPU, 4 GiB, heap 1.5 GiB, page cache 1 GiB), reached
400 users with no failed request and moved the ceiling to the UI. A load run in
between (`20261006-1359-load-aca`) failed on latency because the onboarding
agent was retrying a stuck credential request thirty times a second in the
background (#577); the fix (#581) went out before the evening runs.

### 2026-10-05: the baseline

The first runs against the live hub, from a laptop in Berlin, with the
platform's side from Azure Monitor: [the Azure baseline](/docs/operations/load-test-azure-2026-10-05).
50 users for 15 minutes passed with no failed request but an API p95 of
1.8 s, with `/api/graph` at 10 s; the audited queries hit the proxy's rate
limit (83.6 % 429 before #534, 23.2 % after). Neo4j at 97 % of its 2 GiB was
the first ceiling. The same suite against [the compose stack](/docs/operations/load-test-compose-2026-10-05)
on a laptop, for comparison: load passes every SLO at 50 users, stress breaks
between 100 and 200 users on the UI's CPU.

![Load and stress test dashboard, 50 users against ehds.mabu.red on 2026-10-05](__BASE_PATH__/published-docs/2026-10-05-load-azure.png)

## What the dashboard shows

The **Load and stress test** dashboard (`observability/grafana/dashboards-azure/load-stress-test.json`)
has three rows, each filtered by the run's `testid`:

- **Load (k6): what the test is doing**: virtual users, requests per second,
  failed requests, p95 per group (pages, API, NLQ), the slowest endpoints.
- **Server side: the proxy**: requests and p95 by route, rate-limit refusals,
  the audit chain's records per transaction, the log lines of this run.
- **Containers**: CPU and memory of the UI, the proxy, Neo4j, Keycloak and the
  connectors, replicas, and the Flexible Server's burst credits.

The **EDC contracts and transfers** dashboard (`mvhd-edc-dsp`) follows the
negotiations and transfers a `contracts` run drives through the connectors.
How to read a result, hypothesis by hypothesis, is in the
[runbook](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/knowledge/runbooks/load-and-stress-test.md).

## The runs still to do

1. `stress` after `scripts/azure/size-ui.sh` (ADR-061): where the 1 s API SLO
   first breaks with whole-core replicas; the per-stage p95 goes into the
   ADR's table.
2. `spike`, then `soak` for two hours: the Postgres burst credits (hypothesis
   4 of the runbook) and the cost per 1,000 requests from Cost Management over
   the soak window.
3. `signin` live: whether sign-in is a singleton (hypothesis 6).
4. `load` once more with the EDC pages doing real work (#648 pins the
   connector's address on every deploy).

Each inside office hours, announced, one at a time; a deploy waits while a run
is on. The procedure is the [runbook](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/knowledge/runbooks/load-and-stress-test.md);
the open items are tracked in [#571](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/issues/571).

## Reproduce

```bash
scripts/azure/run-load-test.sh load            # inside Azure, as a Container Apps job
ABORT_ON=failures scripts/azure/run-load-test.sh stress
load-tests/run.sh load azure                   # from a laptop, metrics to a local Grafana
```

The sessions are forged for ten users per persona and handed to the job as a
secret; nothing real signs in. The suite, its scenarios and its thresholds are
documented in [`load-tests/README.md`](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/load-tests/README.md).

docs.markdown:
# Load test baseline, Azure, 2026-10-05 (#519)

Four k6 runs against https://ehds.mabu.red from a laptop in Berlin, inside
office hours, with the suite of `load-tests/` (persona mix, forged sessions, ten
users per persona). Metrics streamed to the local Grafana ("Load and stress
test" dashboard); the platform's side from `scripts/azure/export-load-metrics.sh`
(Azure Monitor, 1-minute grain). Raw data: `load-tests/results/<testid>*` on the
laptop.

The platform that day: UI 1 to 3 replicas at 0.5 vCPU, proxy 1 to 2 at 0.25,
Neo4j 5.26 Community, one replica, 1 vCPU and 2 GiB, Keycloak one replica,
Flexible Server B1ms. ACA's default HTTP rule (10 concurrent requests) scaled
the UI and the proxy.

## Runs

| testid                     | What                                            | Requests | Failed                  | p95 (ms): pages / API / NLQ |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | -------- | ----------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `20261005-smoke-azure`     | 1 user, 30 s                                    | 15       | 0                       | 626 / 221 / -               |
| `20261005-audited-azure`   | 1 → 20 parallel NLQ, one participant, #534 live | 4,871    | 4,071 (83.6 %, all 429) | - / - / 544 (successes)     |
| `20261005-audited-azure-2` | same, #536 live (per user)                      | 4,341    | 1,006 (23.2 %, all 429) | - / - / 434                 |
| `20261005-load-azure`      | 50 users, 15 min, persona mix                   | 16,950   | **0**                   | 546 / **1,800** / 563       |

The dashboard's client-side rows for the two main runs (the server-side and
container rows read the local Loki and Docker, not Azure):

![Load and stress test dashboard, 50 users against ehds.mabu.red](__BASE_PATH__/published-docs/2026-10-05-load-azure.png)

![Load and stress test dashboard, the audited run against ehds.mabu.red](__BASE_PATH__/published-docs/2026-10-05-audited-azure.png)

## The platform during the 50-user run (11:40 to 11:56 UTC)

| App              | Replicas | CPU max | Memory max | Ingress response time, 1-min average max |
| ---------------- | -------- | ------- | ---------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| mvhd-ui          | 3 (max)  | 48 %    | 16 %       | 85 ms                                    |
| mvhd-neo4j-proxy | 2 (max)  | 8 %     | 7 %        | 68 ms                                    |
| mvhd-neo4j       | 1        | 45 %    | **97 %**   | (no ingress)                             |
| mvhd-keycloak    | 1        | 0 %     | 29 %       | 17 ms (no sign-ins in this run)          |
| Flexible Server  |          | 16 %    |            | 23 connections, 64 burst credits         |

Neo4j's CPU rose from 1 % to 41 to 45 % within three minutes of the ramp and
stayed there; its memory sat at 97 % of the 2 GiB limit.

## Per endpoint, 50 users (p95 over the run)

| Endpoint                    | p95        | Requests |
| --------------------------- | ---------- | -------- |
| `GET /api/graph`            | **10.0 s** | 453      |
| `GET /api/compliance`       | 1.8 s      | 419      |
| `GET /api/overview`         | 1.2 s      | 409      |
| `GET /api/catalog`          | 0.69 s     | 1,186    |
| `GET /api/credentials`      | 0.47 s     | 411      |
| `GET /api/participants`     | 0.46 s     | 412      |
| `GET /api/tasks`            | 0.46 s     | 722      |
| `GET /api/analytics`        | 0.45 s     | 726      |
| `GET /api/patient/profile`  | 0.36 s     | 1,095    |
| `GET /api/patient/research` | 0.35 s     | 1,087    |
| `GET /api/patient/insights` | 0.35 s     | 1,090    |
| `GET /api/trust-center`     | 0.29 s     | 418      |
| `POST /api/nlq`             | 0.56 s     | 723      |
| pages (11 routes)           | ≤ 0.55 s   | 7,330    |

## Findings

1. **Rate limit (hypothesis 1), three states in one day.** Per IP (before #534):
   one bucket for the whole platform. Per participant (#534): one organisation's
   20 users exhausted 100 a minute in seconds, 83.6 % refused. Per user (#536):
   the 50-user mix saw no 429 at all; the remaining 23 % in `audited-2` is that
   scenario's shape (20 VUs on 10 users, five questions a second each, no think
   time), not a person's behaviour.
2. **The audit chain (hypothesis 2) is not a ceiling** at the rates reached:
   434 ms p95 at about 16 audited queries a second, with the batch writer live.
3. **Neo4j is the ceiling (hypothesis 5), by memory before CPU.** 97 % of 2 GiB
   during the 50-user run, and the three slow endpoints are the three that read
   the most of the graph: `/api/graph` (the whole knowledge graph, p95 10 s),
   `/api/compliance` and `/api/overview`. Neo4j Community has no cluster mode:
   the options are a larger container (memory first), a smaller or cached answer
   for `/api/graph`, or Enterprise / Aura. Follow-up: #540.
4. **Postgres (hypothesis 4):** 16 % CPU and 64 burst credits at 50 users with
   no sign-ins; the morning start had drawn the credits down to 36 earlier. The
   `signin` and `soak` runs are the ones to measure it.
5. **Sign-in (hypothesis 6):** not exercised live yet; on compose 13 of 13
   sign-ins passed at 310 ms p95 per request.
6. **Scale-out works where it exists:** UI to 3 and proxy to 2 within the ramp,
   both with headroom at 50 users (48 % and 8 % CPU). The `stress` run will find
   the UI's knee; locally one Node process saturated at 50 to 60 requests a
   second, so about 150 users for three replicas, if ACA scales ahead of it.

## Not yet run live

`stress`, `spike`, `soak`, `signin`, `proxy` (internal; needs a job inside the
environment). Each inside office hours, announced, one at a time.

## Reproduce

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.observability.yml up -d
export NEXTAUTH_SECRET="$(az containerapp secret show -n mvhd-ui -g rg-mvhd-dev --secret-name nextauth-secret --query value -o tsv)"
load-tests/run.sh load azure
scripts/azure/export-load-metrics.sh <testid> <start> <end>
```

# Load and stress test, compose stack, 2026-10-05

Issue [#519](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/issues/519). The local
half of the baseline: the k6 suite from `load-tests/` against the JAD compose stack on a
laptop, streamed to the Grafana dashboard "Load and stress test". The live hub's runs are
reported in #519 separately.

## Setup

| What        | Value                                                                                                                   |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Host        | Laptop, Docker Desktop with 10 CPUs and 15.7 GiB                                                                        |
| Stack       | `docker-compose.yml` + `docker-compose.jad.yml`, UI on `:3003`, proxy on `:9090`                                        |
| Images      | `neo4j-proxy` and UI built from `main` at `a06020b` (after #534)                                                        |
| Rate limits | **Lifted for these runs only**: `RATE_LIMIT_MAX` and `RATE_LIMIT_HEAVY_MAX` at 1,000,000. Not the shipped configuration |
| Tool        | k6 2.3.0, metrics by Prometheus remote write, one run at a time                                                         |
| Suite fixes | #537 (persona mix, two dashboard tiles) and #538 (expected 403, POST cohort, failed share, CPU panel)                   |

The rate limit was measured on its own earlier (#534, #536). With it in place a local run
measures the limit, not the platform; these runs measure capacity.

**Noise on the host.** Two data planes crash-loop on this stack (36,000 restarts in five
days, each JVM start taking 2 to 3.5 cores for a few seconds), a kind cluster peaks at 4
cores, and two observability stacks run side by side. The numbers below are therefore
pessimistic, and one stall (below) is the host, not the platform.

## Results

| Run (testid)              | Shape                          | Requests | Failed | p95    | p99    | Verdict                     |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------ | -------- | ------ | ------ | ------ | --------------------------- |
| `20261005-smoke-local`    | 1 user, 1 min                  | 30       | 0 %    | 1.25 s | 2.11 s | cold start after a restart  |
| `20261005-load-local-2`   | 50 users, 15 min, full mix     | 19,216   | 0 %    | 184 ms | 488 ms | **passes every SLO**        |
| `20261005-stress-local-2` | 50 → 100 → 200 → 400 users     | 30,563   | 0 %    | 979 ms | 2.10 s | breaks between 100 and 200  |
| `20261005-audited-local`  | NLQ only, 1 → 20 parallel      | 5,786    | 0 %    | 252 ms | 416 ms | passes                      |
| `20261005-proxy-local-2`  | proxy direct, 5 → 25 users     | 3,531    | 0.06 % | 499 ms | 1.71 s | passes                      |
| `20261005-signin-local`   | Keycloak sign-in, 5 → 50 a min | 889      | 0 %    | 797 ms | 2.54 s | 12 of 127 sign-ins over 3 s |

Load, 50 users: pages p95 97 ms, API p95 220 ms, NLQ p95 211 ms. Slowest endpoint
`GET /api/graph`, p95 587 ms.

### Stress, by stage

| Stage     | Requests / s | Page p95 | API p95  | NLQ p95  | UI CPU (avg / max) | Neo4j CPU (avg / max) |
| --------- | ------------ | -------- | -------- | -------- | ------------------ | --------------------- |
| 50 users  | 24.6         | 93 ms    | 167 ms   | 249 ms   | 32 / 53 %          | 36 / 234 %            |
| 100 users | 48.3         | 267 ms   | 341 ms   | 433 ms   | 60 / 100 %         | 34 / 114 %            |
| 100 → 200 | 70.3         | 1,452 ms | 1,902 ms | 2,338 ms | **86 / 127 %**     | 45 / 91 %             |

k6 stopped the run at 12 min 48 s, at 200 users, when the API p95 passed 1 s. No request
failed at any stage. The slowest endpoints at 200 users: `/api/graph` 3.5 s,
`/api/overview` 2.5 s, `/api/tasks` 2.5 s, `/api/nlq` 2.3 s.

## Findings

1. **The UI is the ceiling, not Neo4j.** Next.js serves from one Node.js process, one event
   loop on one core: at 100 users the UI container reached 100 % of a core and the p95
   started to climb; between 100 and 200 users it stayed at a core while Neo4j used under
   half of one. Locally, one core of UI carries about 50 to 60 requests a second (100
   users at this think time) within the SLOs. On Azure each `mvhd-ui` replica has 0.5 vCPU
   and ACA scales to 3, so the same arithmetic gives roughly 1.5 cores, about 150 users,
   provided the replicas are up before the load; to be checked by the live stress run.
2. **The audit chain keeps up (hypothesis 2).** 5,786 audited queries at up to 42 a
   second, p95 121 ms at one user and 254 ms at 20. The batch writer took up to 18 records
   per transaction, and both chains verified afterwards (`query` 8,975 records, `dsp` 60).
3. **Neo4j is not the ceiling locally (hypothesis 5).** Average 34 to 45 % of a core
   through the stress run. Its stop-the-world pauses (below) were the host.
4. **Keycloak is not the ceiling locally (hypothesis 6).** 127 real sign-ins at up to 50 a
   minute, Keycloak at 20 % average, 71 % at peak, no failures. The 12 slow sign-ins
   coincide with the host's CPU spikes.
5. **A regulator never sees the trust centres.** `/compliance`, the HDAB_AUTHORITY page,
   fetches `/api/trust-center`; the route admits only TRUST_CENTER_OPERATOR and EDC_ADMIN,
   so it answers 403 and the page shows an empty section without an error. Found once the
   persona mix ran the regulator journey (#537). Needs an access decision; the suite now
   expects the 403 (#538).
6. **`/api/tasks` hides two broken backends.** Locally the EDC management API answers 404
   for `/v5alpha/participants` and the proxy's `/tasks` answers 500 ("must be owner of
   table tasks"); the route still answers 200 with mock tasks.
7. **One 60-second stall, from the host.** In the first load run every in-flight request
   waited 60 s between 10:05:47 and 10:06:49 UTC. Neo4j logged JVM pauses of up to 23.7 s
   with no garbage collection, and the proxy logged nothing for that minute: the Docker VM
   was not scheduled. The rerun had no stall.

## Bugs in the suite and the dashboard, found by these runs

| Bug                                                                                   | Fixed in |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| VUs 1 to 50 were all patients and researchers (`vu % 100`)                            | #537     |
| "Failed requests" read 100 % (max over per-status rate series)                        | #537     |
| "Checks passed" showed the best check, not the worst                                  | #537     |
| "Failed requests" counted the expected 403                                            | #538     |
| "CPU by container" barely moved under load (lifetime ratio); now the CPU time counter | #538     |
| The proxy scenario sent `GET /omop/cohort`; the route is `POST`                       | #538     |

## Dashboards

Grafana "Load and stress test", one run per `testid`:

- Stress: `http://localhost:3301/d/mvhd-load-test/load-and-stress-test?var-testid=20261005-stress-local-2&from=1791195600000&to=1791196440000`
- Load: `http://localhost:3301/d/mvhd-load-test/load-and-stress-test?var-testid=20261005-load-local-2&from=1791196440000&to=1791197400000`
- Audited: `http://localhost:3301/d/mvhd-load-test/load-and-stress-test?var-testid=20261005-audited-local&from=1791197400000&to=1791197760000`

The port is the second observability stack's (`:3301`), which holds these runs and the
live hub's; the default stack serves the same dashboard on `:3300`.

### Stress, 50 → 200 users

![Stress run](__BASE_PATH__/published-docs/2026-10-05-stress-local.png)

### Load, 50 users, 15 minutes

![Load run](__BASE_PATH__/published-docs/2026-10-05-load-local.png)

### Audited queries, 1 → 20 parallel

![Audited run](__BASE_PATH__/published-docs/2026-10-05-audited-local.png)

## Reproduce

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.observability.yml up -d
load-tests/run.sh load local       # TESTID=... to name the run
load-tests/run.sh stress local
load-tests/run.sh audited local
```

The runbook is [`docs/knowledge/runbooks/load-and-stress-test.md`](https://github.com/ma3u/MinimumViableHealthDataspacev2/blob/main/docs/knowledge/runbooks/load-and-stress-test.md).
